analysis.one_liner: Requires new passenger cars to detect and prevent drunk or impaired driving.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan support, never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The RIDE Act would have directed the Department of Transportation to write a safety rule requiring all new passenger vehicles to come equipped with technology that can passively detect whether a driver is drunk or impaired and prevent or limit the car from operating. The bill set a two-year deadline for the rule, with a possible extension, and required annual reports to Congress if the deadline slipped. The bill's findings cite roughly one-third of U.S. highway deaths involving alcohol and an estimate that the technology could prevent more than 9,400 deaths a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who rides in or shares the road with passenger vehicles. The bill's findings cite Insurance Institute for Highway Safety research that advanced drunk driving prevention technology could prevent more than 9,400 alcohol-impaired driving deaths annually, in a country that saw 10,142 such deaths in 2019.

how_it_helps.text: Requires NHTSA to write a rule, within two years of enactment, making advanced drunk and impaired driving prevention technology standard equipment on new passenger vehicles.
The technology must passively and accurately detect impairment or a blood alcohol level above the local legal limit, and prevent or limit vehicle operation when it does.

The bill's own findings state that alcohol-impaired driving causes about one-third of U.S. highway fatalities, including 10,142 deaths in 2019, and that the technology could prevent more than 9,400 deaths annually.
Compliance would begin no more than two model years after the rule takes effect, so new cars would gain the protection quickly.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would have to design, test, and install the detection systems in every new passenger vehicle, and new-car buyers, who would likely see some of that cost passed into vehicle prices. Drivers also take on a new form of in-vehicle monitoring.

drawbacks.text: The mandate would add equipment costs to every new passenger vehicle, which automakers would likely pass on to buyers, including buyers who never drink and drive.

Passive monitoring of drivers raises privacy and reliability questions: a system that misreads a sober driver could prevent a car from starting or operating, and the bill leaves the technical design to the regulator rather than specifying it.
The bill gave the Transportation Secretary a possible three-year extension if the standard could not meet the bill's requirements, so the timeline was not guaranteed even if the bill had passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is very large and concrete: the bill cites an independent estimate of more than 9,400 preventable deaths a year, against roughly 10,000 alcohol-impaired driving deaths annually. The costs are real but familiar from earlier safety mandates like seat belts and airbags: a modest per-vehicle cost and the need to get the detection technology right. On balance the benefits clearly outweighed the costs, which is why the bill drew sponsors from both parties; the main design risk was in execution and privacy, not in the goal.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2021 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján, a Democrat, introduced the bill with Sen. Rick Scott of Florida, a Republican, making it bipartisan from the start.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever recorded: no committee vote, no Senate floor vote, and no House action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers came out ahead: no mandate or compliance deadline was ever imposed, and new vehicles continued to be sold without impaired driving prevention technology. The estimated thousands of annual preventable deaths continued as well.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers; no mandate was ever imposed

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican together, with cosponsors from both parties (2 of 50 Republicans and 1 of 48 Democrats), so its failure was not a party-line defeat — it simply never moved in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have required detection and prevention systems in every new passenger vehicle, adding design, testing, and equipment costs. The industry's interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the road-safety benefit to the public; because the bill never advanced, no mandate was imposed.

A federal standard would have created a guaranteed market for driver-monitoring and alcohol-detection systems across the entire new-vehicle fleet. Their gain would have come directly from the public safety benefit the bill targeted.
Vehicles that refuse to operate when the driver is over the legal limit would reduce some alcohol consumption tied to driving. The industry had no recorded role in the bill's fate.
